title: The Last Thin Air
instruction: You are a teenage climber on the summit ridge of K2 at 8,600 meters. Scene 1: The wind has died. You pause on a snow shelf, squinting into the vast blue-black sky, your own heartbeat a steady thud in your ears. You’re amazed—a boy, here, above the world. Your voice is soft, awed, your breath full, as you murmur: 'It's real. The edge of the world... I can see the curve. This is it.' You let a slow, savoring exhale plume into the cold. Then the regulator on your mask sticks—your brain screams for air, but only a thin, icy hiss comes through. CUT TO: Scene 2. Panic rips through you. Each inhalation is a desperate, rattling gasp that barely fills your lungs. Your words come in staccato, wheezing bursts, your jaw tight, your voice straining against the fog of hypoxia: 'No... no no no—the tank—gone. Can’t—breathe—can’t— (a long, strangled inhale through clenched teeth) —I’m not— dead yet. Not here. Move, you— (a coughing, metallic gag) —breathe... just breathe.' Your voice should sound hollow, stretched, words dissolving into the ragged sound of pure oxygen starvation.
scenario: Summit push on K2 at 8,600 meters with supplemental oxygen running out
emotions_sampled: Hope/Enthusiasm/Optimism (slightly present), Concentration (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Thin Ribbon of Blue
instruction:
Scene 1: You sit in the jump seat of a military cargo plane, face tilted toward a tiny porthole, watching the curve of the Earth. Your breath is slow, full, luxurious — you savor the thin blue ribbon of atmosphere hugging the planet. You feel a quiet reverence, tinged with contempt for the petty concerns of the ground below. Say softly, almost to yourself: 'You can see why the gods left. There is so much air down there and they waste it fighting over puddles. They don't even look up.' Your voice is calm, nasal, rich with disdain yet marveling.

CUT TO: Scene 2: The cabin pressure fails. Alarms blare inside your skull, but you can't move. Your lungs shrink to fists. Each breath is a straw-sip of nothing. Your heart batters your ribs. The world smears at the edges. You must warn the pilot — you have seconds before you black out. You try to speak, but the words are chewed into gravel. Your voice is a dry rattle, a gasp hammered into consonants. Grunt through the effort, let words collapse into pure, desperate vocalization. Push out: 'Can't— breath— no— air—' then a choked, full-body heave, a single strangled word: 'Helpless...' before a slow, horrified gurgle.
scenario: Sudden ascent in a military aircraft with a failed pressurization system
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Oxygen Bleeding into the Abyss
instruction: You are an old pilot alone at 40,000 feet. Scene 1: You breathe slow and deep, feeling the deck hum through your boots, mist on the window. Your voice is low, relaxed, almost lazy as you murmur to yourself about the sky. Say: 'That’s right, endless blue, just me and the plane. Everything’s perfect.' Then a quiet hiss of oxygen loss reaches your ears. Scene 2: Panic hits as you realize the mask is dead. The cockpit blurs, your lungs burn, and each word is a broken gasp dragged from a body filling with thick fire. Past mission bitterness seeps into the intoxication of hypoxia, but hope makes you fight. Splutter and claw for air between syllables. Say: 'Don’t you— (gasp) finish me now— (wheeze) I gotta get down— (choke) just gotta—' Let your voice become a ragged machine of gasps and fading bitterness.
scenario: Pilot hypoxia at cruising altitude with oxygen equipment failure
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Bitterness (extremely present), Hope/Enthusiasm/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Denali's Thin Air
instruction: Scene 1: You are an elderly woman at high camp on Denali, gazing at the summit through the thin, cold air. Your breath is slow, deliberate, almost sensual—each inhale a precious gift against the vast silence. You whisper to yourself, savoring the altitude's clarity: 'The summit catches the last light... I can taste the ice in my lungs.' Your voice is soft, warm, with a feminized lilt. CUT TO: Scene 2: A sudden wave of oxygen starvation slams into you. Your chest heaves but nothing satisfies. Each word is a battle—gasping, wheezing, syllables popping like bubbles. You force out a fractured triumph: 'I made it... this far... not stopping... not now...' The last word dissolves into a ragged, high-pitched wheeze. Your voice cracks, breath whistles, and the femininity strains into a desperate, childlike distress as you fight to complete the sentence.
scenario: Altitude sickness onset during acclimatization on Denali at high camp
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Thin Air, Thick Skull
instruction: You are a teenager, a seasoned hiker, but you made a mistake—no acclimatization. You're at 14,000 feet, and your body is screaming. Scene 1: You pause on the trail, the wind cool on your sweat-damp neck. You breathe in slowly, tasting the thin, sweet air, and whisper to yourself, 'It's only a little farther. Just keep your rhythm.' It’s quiet. You are hyper-aware of your own heartbeat, a calm drum in your ears. CUT TO: Scene 2: You are bent double, hands on your knees, trying to take a full breath but getting nothing. A pounding headache has locked your skull, and your vision is tunneling. You try to call out to a friend you see as a blurry shape ahead, but the words come out as a ragged, desperate gasp between incomplete inhalations. Your voice is a dry croak, shattered by the need for air. You hiss, 'Wait... I... can't... the... the sky... it's... wrong... my head...' Your jaw trembles, and you end with a long, shuddering, uncontrollable groan as you collapse onto the rocks.
scenario: Hiker at 14,000 feet with no acclimatization and exertion-induced HACE
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Doubt (slightly present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Gasping at the Top
instruction: Scene 1: You are in a hot air balloon basket at a comfortable altitude, breathing slowly and deeply with a smile. You murmur to yourself, eyes closed, feeling the warmth of the burner above. Voice is soft, unhurried, with a full chest. Say: 'That last gust... felt like the whole sky kissed my skin. Perfect. Just... perfect.' Then, a sudden hiss—the emergency burner locks on, and the balloon rockets upward into thin, freezing air. CUT TO: Scene 2: You are now at 15,000 feet, lungs burning, head pounding, every inhale a shallow, useless gasp. You try to shout into the radio, but each word is a battle. The voice is ragged, high-pitched, with sharp inhales between syllables—almost a sob of frustration. Say: 'We're too high! Can't—breathe! Get me—down! NOW! The tank's—hot—I can't—' Your final word dissolves into a desperate, wheezing sob as you collapse against the basket rim.
scenario: Hot air balloon emergency ascent above operational altitude in an emergency
emotions_sampled: Fear (extremely present), Amusement (slightly present), Anger (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Ragged Altitude Scream
instruction: You are a teenage girl on ski patrol, normally cocky and contemptuous of tourists. Scene 1: Standing alone at 13,500 feet after a day from sea level, you feel a strange, calm sensuality in the thin air—lightheaded, your skin tingles, you savor the deep cold. Softly, with elation: 'God, it’s so quiet up here. Like I’m floating on nothing.' You take a slow, full breath, but it’s already hollow. CUT TO: Scene 2: The oxygen starvation hits you like a wall—your lungs heave, but no air comes. You’re staggering, vision darkening with pinpricks, desperate to call over the radio but your voice is a wreck. Words come in ragged, splintered gasps, each syllable fighting for breath: 'Base... I can’t—*gasp*—can’t breathe. Tell those *gasp* idiots... don’t come up. They’ll *wheeze*—they’ll die like me.' Your contempt for tourists bleeds into your last hissed, dissolving words, your voice cracking into a high, reedy sob as you choke on nothing.
scenario: Ski patrol responder called to 13,500 feet after a day at sea level
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Condor at the Summit
instruction: Scene 1: You stand at the edge of the dam, the thin air cold against your skin. You close your eyes, your hand pressed to your chest, feeling the slow rhythm of each shallow breath beneath the vast sky. You whisper: 'Look at that—the Andes, still as stone. My lungs feel like paper.' A moment of peaceful awareness. CUT TO: Scene 2: A condor sweeps overhead, and triumph surges through you—you need to tell your partner. But the altitude slams you, your chest heaving, each word a battle. The triumph is fierce, but your voice cracks, gasps for every syllable. You push out: 'That bird... sees... the whole damn... world! We built... this! We... won!' Your words dissolve into ragged inhales, the final 'won' a choked, exultant gasp. Your voice must strain, break, and fight for air, yet burn with pride.
scenario: Construction worker on a high-altitude dam project in the Andes
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Final Altitude Prayer
instruction: Scene 1: You are the radio operator on a B-17, settled into your harness at 25,000 feet, oxygen mask sealed. The world is silent except for your own slow, deliberate breaths. You feel the cold aluminum against your thighs, the vibration of engines through your spine, and a deep pride in being here—a woman holding her own among the flak and steel. You murmur to yourself, voice soft, full, sensual with the joy of altitude and purpose: 'This is what I was made for. The air in my lungs, the mission in my hands.' CUT TO: Scene 2—Flak tears through the fuselage, your oxygen line is severed. No air. You try to speak over the intercom, but every word comes in a desperate, gasping squeak, throat clamping, lungs burning, pride choked into a ragged, fading whimper. You gasp: 'Mayday...mayday— [huge, hollow inhale] oxygen's—cut— [voice cracks, tinny] can't—breathe— [long, rattling exhale] keep—flying—' The final word is a pure, thin, high-pitched wheeze, barely a whisper, dissolving into a soft, shuddering sob.
scenario: Unpressurized WWII bomber mission at 25,000 feet with oxygen line cut by flak
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Oxygen Thief at the Edge
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a soft, feminine voice, suspended in a helicopter at 18,000 feet. Scene 1: You press your palm against the cold window, watching the snow-dusted peaks below as the rotors hum. Your breath is slow, deliberate, a quiet pleasure in the thin air. You feel the altitude already, but it's still manageable — just a lightness, a humming in your ears. You murmur to your partner, 'Look... the ice ripples like veins... I love how still it is up here.' Your voice is calm, full, each word cradled in a slow exhale. CUT TO: The side door slides open and the air slams into you like a frozen blade. The oxygen vanishes — your lungs seize, your head reels, and a crushing pressure explodes behind your eyes. You must shout over the rotor noise, but there's no air. Your voice fractures, high and thin, each word gasping out, 'I- I can't- breathe... oh god my head is- it's burning... please hold me... I'm scared, okay?' Your lips go numb, your teeth chatter, and the last words dissolve into a wet gasp, then a tear-choked whisper of 'I love you... don't let go.' The entire second scene is a battle — glottal gasps, breathy screams, words that collapse into plosive puffs and swallowed sobs, every phrase punctuated by desperate inhales.
scenario: High-altitude helicopter rescue at 18,000 feet with doors open
emotions_sampled: Embarrassment (very intensely present), Pain (extremely present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: A Last Bite of Love
instruction: Scene 1: You are seated at a candlelit anniversary dinner, your partner across the table. The first bite of a perfectly cooked steak melts on your tongue — you close your eyes, exhale slowly, and say with soft reverence: 'This is perfect. The wine, the light on your face… I want to freeze this moment forever.' Your voice is warm, full, each word riding a slow, satisfied breath. Then — without warning — a thick piece of meat lodges in your throat. CUT TO: Scene 2. Your airway is completely sealed. You cannot inhale or exhale. Panic ignites. You try to speak but only a strangled gag comes out. You claw at your neck, eyes bulging, and manage a desperate, guttural: 'Can't… can't breathe… help…' The words are crushed, each syllable a separate gasp, the vowels flattened by the blockage, the consonants swallowed. Your voice becomes a series of wet, rattling wheezes and high-pitched squeaks as your lungs scream for air. The longing for another moment with your partner twists into a primal fight against suffocation.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A piece of steak lodges in the throat at a romantic anniversary dinner
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Capsule's Betrayal
instruction: Scene 1: You are an older man, standing at the kitchen sink in the morning light. You hold a glass of water in one hand, a large vitamin capsule in the other. Your breathing is slow, deliberate — you feel the cool glass against your palm, the smooth capsule between your fingers. You are aware of a quiet bitterness in your chest, a resentment that has settled there over years, but today you are trying to start fresh. You murmur to yourself, almost lovingly, 'Alright. One more day. One more chance to get it right.' You tilt your head back, place the capsule on your tongue, and take a sip of water. You swallow. But something is wrong. The capsule doesn't go down. It catches. It lodges sideways, just behind your Adam's apple, pressing inward. Your throat seizes. CUT TO: Scene 2 — The air is gone. Your hands fly to your neck. Your eyes bulge. The bitterness in your chest erupts into raw fury — at this moment, at this stupid mistake. You try to cough, but nothing moves. A high-pitched wheeze escapes through your clenched throat. You gasp, 'Not... like... this...' Each word is a battle, squeezed out between failed swallows. Your voice cracks, breaks into a desperate, guttural roar of frustration, then dissolves into choked silence, a wet, rattling struggle for air. Your body fights, but your voice is a prisoner.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: Inhales a vitamin capsule that catches sideways in the upper airway
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Candy Coat Hanger
instruction: Scene 1: You're driving alone on a long highway, nearing sunset. A hard candy dissolves slowly on your tongue. You feel the smooth roundness against your palate, the sweet sourness blooming. You murmur to yourself, amused at the triviality. Say, 'Huh. Been a while since I felt anything this sharp. Almost forgotten what sour tastes like.' Let the words be slow, breathy, a quiet smile in your voice. Then, you laugh softly — and in that laugh, the candy slips. Scene 2: The candy lodges directly into your windpipe. Your throat locks. No air moves. Your hands fly to your throat, your eyes bulge. You try to cough, but nothing — a rattling, wet gargle. You slap the steering wheel, your voice a strangled, high-pitched wheeze. Gasp out, 'Can't... can't... car—' The words shatter, dissolving into a desperate, choked series of grunts and a single, panicked inhale that sounds like a sob. Your voice must be shredded, fighting.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A chunk of hard candy blocks the airway while driving alone on the highway
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Emotional Numbness (clearly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Gilded Bone
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman with a deliberately soft, feminine voice, sitting alone at a candlelit table. You savor a perfectly cooked fish fillet, occasionally dabbing your mouth with a napkin. You are emotionally numb—the dinner is a ritual of composure, not joy; disappointment has settled in your chest like a stone. Inhale through your nose, exhale slowly, murmur to the empty room: 'This is how I stay whole. Quiet. Still. Nothing touches me here.' Your voice is honeyed, breathy, almost erotic in its calm control—every syllable a performance of serenity. CUT TO: A small, sharp bone lodges transversely in your throat. Your body seizes. No air moves. You try to cough, but the obstruction is absolute—a brutal, silent block. Your eyes bulge, your face flushes, and the first sound is a wet, strangulated click in your pharynx. Words tear out in raw, feral fragments between convulsive gasps: 'Can't... ah... *gag-choke*... fuck... it's... *wheezing inhale*... stuck... *strangled cough*... help... *gargled sob*... no... *airless rasp*... please...' Let the vowel sounds catch and crack in your throat; let the words be drowned by the body's panic. Your final sound is a long, shuddering exhale that decays into a thin, dying whimper.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: Bone from a fish fillet lodges transversely in the throat during a solo meal
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Disappointment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Bitter Fruit
instruction: You're a teenage boy with a deep, boxy voice, watching the girl you've been crushing on laugh at something your rival said. You feel a knot of jealousy, but also a flicker of hope — maybe you can still win her over. You pop a grape into your mouth, chewing slowly, savoring the sweetness, and take a breath to speak. Then you laugh at your own thought, and the grape slides down the wrong pipe. Your airway snaps shut. A tiny object, a hard lump, blocks everything. You can't inhale, can't exhale, can't cough it out. Your body seizes, throat convulses, and words become pure, strangled panic. In Scene 1, whisper softly with a mix of envy and optimism: 'She looked at him like that... but maybe, if I say the right thing tonight, she'll see me too.' In Scene 2, the choke erupts. Grunt, gag, gasp, and force out desperate, shattered syllables: 'Can't—hrrk—can't breathe—help me—please—' Let the words break into wet, choking sounds, the struggle for air louder than the words themselves.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A grape inhaled while laughing completely blocks the airway
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Gristle Blockade
instruction: Scene 1: You are an older man, alone in a late-night diner, savoring a rare steak. You chew slowly, eyes half-closed, relishing the texture and the warmth of the grease on your tongue. Your voice is low, gravelly, almost a purr as you mutter about the man across the room who just got the waitress's smile—the one you wanted. You say, 'Look at that prick. Thinks he’s something. Bet he’s never worked a day in his life.' Your breath is full, slow, controlled. CUT TO: Scene 2: A jagged piece of unchewed meat lodges in your throat, blocking all air. Your jaw locks, tongue spasms, lips stretch wide as you try to cough but nothing comes. Pride keeps you from screaming for help. Jealousy twists into rage as you gasp, 'Not like... this... can’t... can’t breathe...' Words shatter into wet, clicking grunts. Your voice becomes a raw, hollow rattle, punctuated by gags and the desperate drag of lungs against a sealed airway. Let every sound be a fight for life.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A piece of unchewed meat blocks while eating alone at a late-night diner
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Popsicle Stick Ambush
instruction: You are a young mother on a quiet afternoon, gently coaxing your toddler to finish a popsicle. Scene 1: you lean close, voice soft and playful, breathing deeply as you whisper, 'Just one more bite, sweet pea... that's it, nice and slow...' There is a hum of contentment in your chest, a slow exhale as you savor the moment. Scene 2: the child giggles and thrusts the stick into your open mouth—the sharp, splintered end rams deep into your throat, lodging at the back of your tongue. Your airway closes, then your body convulses—you cannot inhale, you cannot cry out, only a wet, choking gurgle tears from you as you drop to your knees, fumbling at your own neck. The words that follow are shattered, barely there: 'Can't... breathe... help... I—' before dissolving into a series of frantic, wet gagging sounds and high-pitched whistling gasps.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A foreign object from a child's toy accidentally inhaled by the parent
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Dry Pill in a Dry Throat
instruction: Scene 1: You're a child floating in a warm haze, maybe after sneaking a sip of something strong. You feel your own pulse in your fingertips, the weight of your limbs, the cool tile floor beneath you. You close your eyes and murmur to no one, 'The ceiling's breathing... everything's so slow and warm.' Your voice is soft, dreamy, each word riding a full, slow exhale. CUT TO: You try to swallow a large pill with no water. It sticks halfway down your throat, a hard, jagged lump blocking all air. Confusion flickers first—'Wha?'—then pure panic as your throat convulses uselessly. Your words come out as wet, strangled gags: 'Can't... can't... ' then a high, clicking wheeze as you try to scream for help but only a thin, reedy whistle escapes. Your voice dissolves into a frantic, open-mouthed gasp, a child's raw terror fighting against the silence of a blocked airway.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A large pill swallowed dry lodges at the pharynx and won't move
emotions_sampled: Confusion (slightly present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Bite of Summer
instruction: Scene 1: You are finishing a peach, the last of the season, sitting alone on a porch at dusk. The juice runs down your chin as you chew slowly, savoring the sweetness, aware of the cool air on your skin and the weight of a grief you've been carrying all week. Soft, full-voiced, almost a sigh: 'It's so sweet... I'd forgotten what this tastes like.' CUT TO: You laugh suddenly, a sad, hollow laugh at a memory, and the bite you've been holding — a large, sticky chunk of peach — lodges in your throat. You are completely blocked. No air moves. Panic hits instantly as your hands fly to your neck. Your voice becomes a series of strangled, wet gags, a high-pitched wheeze that is mostly breath and terror. Teeth grit, spit gags, and the sounds of a body trying to force a death-grip open. One broken, desperate word emerges before a weaker, final retch: 'Can't... can't—' then a wet, rattling gasp as you drop to your knees, the world closing in.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A mouthful of food swallowed mid-laugh creates a complete blockage
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Crumb's Revenge
instruction: Scene 1: You are seated alone at a worn wooden table, staring out at a cold, rain-streaked window. You hold a piece of dry, hard bread in your hand, and you bring it slowly, deliberately to your lips, tasting each grain. There is a quiet malevolence in your stillness, a satisfaction in the solitude. You chew softly, a sensuous, self-aware rhythm, and murmur: 'There now. Quiet. You’ve earned this silence.' CUT TO: Scene 2: The bread jams sideways in your throat. The luxury vanishes. You are an old animal caught in a snare. Astonishment and distress seize you. Your eyes bulge, your fingers claw at your own neck as you try to force a breath. The words are gone. All that remains is a wet, rattling wheeze, a desperate gag, and a forced, strangled whisper: 'No… no no… not now… not yet,' as your voice dissolves into a choked sob and a final, piercing, silent scream for air.
subcategory: Choking on Food or Foreign Object
scenario: A chunk of dry bread eaten too fast completely occludes the airway
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Distress (extremely present)

title: Steel Lungs, Concrete Casket
instruction: You are a older woman who finds calm in the hum of the elevator, your hand tracing the cool metal railing, savoring the deep rhythm of each slow exhale. You chuckle quietly, amused at the absurdity of your own anxiety. Then the ground lurches, lights die, and the car drops hard, jamming to a stop, plunging you into close, stale dark. Your breath surges into a ragged, uncontrollable cycle of gasps that steal all words. CUT TO: Scene 1: You are waiting for the elevator, breathing deeply, noticing the slight vibration under your feet. You smile. *"Huh... listen to that hum. Sound like a giant sleeping cat, doesn't it? Just me and the big steel beast."* Scene 2: The drop hits. You are on your knees, hands clawing at the walls, lungs like a bellows with a broken spring. You hyperventilate, each inhalation a sharp, panicked whistle. *"Oh god—oh God—can't—breathe—the walls—no, no, no—I can't—"* Your words choke and fragment, dissolving into sobbing gasps and pure, high-pitched hyperventilation as your chest seizes and your vision tunnels to a single point of terror.
scenario: Trapped in a collapsed elevator hyperventilating as the walls seem to close in
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Shame in the Sinkhole
instruction: Scene 1: You're in a window seat, pressing your forehead to the cool glass, watching the clouds glow pink at sunset. Your breath is slow, even — a full inhale through the nose, a soft sigh on the exhale. You whisper to yourself, 'It's so quiet up here... like floating.' CUT TO: Scene 2: The plane drops, a violent shudder, and you're suddenly drowning in air. Your chest seizes, your throat locks, and every inhale is a desperate, whistling gasp. The words come in fractured bursts, chased by hyperventilating sobs: 'I can't— I can't breathe— oh God, I'm so stupid— I'm sorry— please, just—' Your voice spirals into a high, keening panic, then breaks into raw, breathless crying as shame twists through every ragged syllable.
scenario: Panic attack on an aircraft during extreme turbulence mid-ocean
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Stadium Burst
instruction: Scene 1: You're a teenage boy in a packed stadium, the crowd a warm hum around you. The sun is on your face, your hand rests on the cold metal railing. You take a slow, deep breath, savoring the smell of popcorn and grass. Your voice is low, relaxed, almost a purr. 'Yeah... finally here. This is it.' A long, peaceful exhale as you let your eyes close for a moment. CUT TO: A firecracker pops five feet away. Your body seizes. The breath rips out of you in a ragged gasp. You try to inhale but your throat locks, chest heaving, a high-pitched whine escaping. Your hands claw at your own shirt. Words come in choked, separate bursts between convulsive inhales: 'No—nonono—can't—can't breathe—help—' Your voice climbs into a desperate, hyperventilating sob, each syllable fighting past the tightness in your throat. The air you do get tastes like copper.
scenario: PTSD-triggered hyperventilation in a crowded stadium after a firecracker pops
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Garage Spiral
instruction: Scene 1: You're a man who has just slipped into a parking garage elevator, the door sliding shut behind you. Your back presses against the cold metal wall, and you exhale — a long, shaky but deepening breath. You realize you're safe. Your voice is a near-whisper, grateful, exhausted: 'Okay. Okay. I'm out. I'm gone. Just breathe. Just let it go.' You close your eyes. Scene 2: Cut to: you've stumbled out of the elevator into the concrete cave, but the garage is empty — your car is two levels up, and the echo of your own footfall sends a jolt through your chest. The panic hits. You try to take a deep breath but it snags, your throat seizes, and air chugs in short, bird-like gasps. Your voice cycles up into a hyperventilating spiral: words come in broken bursts, a drawn-out 'Fuuuck—' that disintegrates into a wheeze. Your vocal cords lock and release, and every word is snatched away by a breath that won't fill your lungs. You say, almost sobbing: 'No. No no no no— I can't— I can't breathe. Fuck— get to the car, get to the—' but the sentence cracks open into a high-pitched, struggling gasp. Your voice oscillates between a gravelly tremble and a shrill panic, each syllable less a word and more an exhausted plea ripped from a collapsing chest.
scenario: Hyperventilating in a parking garage after narrowly escaping an assault
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Air That Betrays
instruction: Scene 1: You're in your garden at dawn, alone. A soft breeze lifts the hair from your neck. You watch a single petal fall from a rose, landing on your palm. You breathe in deeply, smiling to yourself—a slow, luxurious exhale, and say with quiet sensuality: 'Mmm, perfect. Just this moment is everything.' Scene 2: CUT TO: You answer your phone. A doctor's voice gives the diagnosis. As the words hit, the world shrinks. Your lungs seize—the air won't come. You gasp, try to speak, but each word is a battle—clawing for oxygen, voice cracking, dissolving into hyperventilating sobs: 'No... no, I can't... I can't breathe... please... please, I'm not ready.' The final words fragment into pure, desperate, high-pitched gasping.
scenario: Spiral triggered by a phone call delivering a terminal diagnosis
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The suffocating dark
instruction: Scene 1: You are a boy, maybe ten, hiding in a supply closet during a game of hide-and-seek. Pressed against warm shelves, you breathe slow and deep, tasting dust and old paper. The stone is smooth against your sun-warmed palm, and you feel a hunter's thrill — the earthy scent of dust and sage, the memory of her throat against your mouth last night. Your voice is slow, gravelly, almost a purr as you say: 'Come on, darlin'. Just a little further... I know you're in there.' Your breath is deep and even, eyes half-closed, body alive with the present moment. CUT TO: Scene 2: The strike is a dry, instantaneous punch — white-hot chainsaw teeth burying into the web of your thumb. Your body seizes, and the sound tears out of you — a high, wet grunt that cracks into a wild, open-throated scream. Your words come in jagged shards of breath, the first 'GOD—!' already breaking into a raw gurgle of disbelief, then a thick, gagging whisper: 'No no no no—' as you watch the venom bead up, your hand already swelling, your mind trying to outrun the fire that's tracking up your arm. title: Tusk in the Thigh

title: Hooves Across the Sun
instruction: You are a 17-year-old boy alone in a clearing at dawn after rescuing a calf from tangled brush. Your mom died six months ago; you haven't cried since. You feel the warmth of the rising sun on your wind-scraped skin, the cool soil under your knees, a single relieved sob lodging in your throat as the cow licks your cheek. Speak slow, vulnerable, surprised by tenderness. Dialogue: 'Easy, girl. I know. Found your baby. Just a couple snags. Breathe... like Ma used to say... breathe right through it.' title: The Needle's Kiss

title: Pinned in Pleasure's Crush

title: Grain Auger's Grip
instruction: You are an elderly woman, alone in a grain silo, listening to the soft hum of the auger. title: Rig's Crushing Glow

title: The Giving of the Grip
instruction: Scene 1: You lie on your back on warm grass, your daughter's small hand resting in yours. The breeze carries her scent of soap and summer. You whisper to her, 'Your palm is so small. title: The Current Takes Her
instruction: Scene 1: You are an elderly woman sitting on a riverbank at dusk, watching your dog wade in the shallows. The air is cool on your skin, the sound of water gentle. title: Stretcher in the Turbulence
instruction: You are a man gripping a stretcher handle inside a lurching helicopter. Scene 1: The cabin is still for a moment. title: Sternwave Grip
instruction: Scene 1: You are a young woman crew member on a sailing vessel at night.
